summary:
Suriname has not criminalised consensual same-sex conduct since 1869. In March 2015 the Penal Code was amended so that Articles 175, 175a and 176 reach discrimination and hate speech grounded in sexual orientation, and a revision carried out after the 2011 Universal Periodic Review equalised the age of consent for same-sex and opposite-sex relations.

Protection rests on an implied reading rather than an explicit statute. Article 8.2 of the Surinamese Constitution lists 'any other status' among prohibited grounds, and the government treats that clause as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity. No statutory instrument enumerates sexual orientation or gender identity as protected grounds, and the LGBT Platform Suriname has repeatedly called for a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

Legal gender recognition is not available in Suriname. A trans visitor holding documents in a name or sex marker that does not match their presentation has no domestic procedure through which those documents can be aligned.

Formal guarantees have not removed daily exposure. A joint submission by LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata to the UN Human Rights Committee records that LGBTI people face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatization despite constitutional protection, and the US State Department's 2015 human rights report on Suriname documents discrimination against LGBTI persons and other minorities.

Before the Human Rights Committee in July 2024, Suriname's delegation asserted that national laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, citing monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission. Committee experts pressed the delegation on implementation of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' judgment concerning transgender identity, and that implementation remains open.

Civil society space exists on paper: LGBTI organisations can register in Suriname, and the LGBT Platform Suriname was founded on 29 August 2011.
tangentialFactors:
Reporting to and protection from the police is not a neutral option. The US State Department's 2015 report on Suriname records police brutality and corruption alongside its findings on LGBTI discrimination, alongside coverage of the Bouterse trial, which situates the security forces in a contested political environment.

The state's own account and the account of civil society diverge. Suriname's delegation told the Human Rights Committee in July 2024 that its laws protect against discrimination on sexual orientation, while UN submissions filed by local groups record ongoing discrimination, violence and stigmatization. The gap between the asserted framework and the reported experience is itself a factor for a visitor assessing how much protection is real.

Because constitutional coverage of gender identity and sexual orientation is implied through 'any other status' rather than enumerated in statute, the strength of the protection depends on how courts and administrations choose to read it. Jurisdictions that name the grounds outright leave a visitor less dependent on that interpretive discretion.
localsOnly:
The LGBT Platform Suriname unites five member organisations: PAREA, New Monday Foundation, Suriname Men United, Women's Way and Trans in Action. It was established on 29 August 2011 as an umbrella body.

The Platform has pressed for a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability, and has repeatedly sought inclusion in state consultative processes without being admitted to them.

Registration of LGBTI organisations is permitted, and Trans in Action operates within the Platform as a trans-specific member group.

The government's monitoring apparatus includes bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission, which the delegation cited in July 2024 as part of its discrimination-monitoring framework.

Constitutional Article 8 covers sexual orientation and gender identity only implicitly, and the July 2024 Human Rights Committee review indicates that the state's protection claim rests on that implied reading rather than on enacted anti-discrimination legislation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no entry, visa or border-screening procedure specific to trans travellers entering Suriname, and no information on whether documents are inspected against presentation at airports or land crossings. This is unresolved rather than cleared.

No data is sourced on trans-specific killings or assaults in Suriname with dates, perpetrators or outcomes, so the pattern of lethal violence cannot be assessed from this inventory.

Facilities law, access to hormones and transition-related healthcare, and any hate-crime sentencing enhancement beyond the March 2015 Penal Code discrimination and hate-speech provisions are not sourced here. Whether those Penal Code articles have been used in prosecutions is not recorded.

The content of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' judgment on transgender identity, the precise measures the Human Rights Committee experts asked Suriname to implement in July 2024, and the current status of that implementation are unresolved on this record.

The enforceability of the 'any other status' clause before Surinamese courts, and whether a trans litigant could rely on it in practice, are not sourced.
